li.a: The Age: Bulgarian Nick dies in flurry of shots (17 April 2003)
The Age: Why gangland's bloody code is hard to crack (20 April 2003)
The Age: New lead in Bulgarian Nik's killing (13 December 2003)
The Age: Wise guys, tough guys, dead guys (14 December 2003)
The Age: Six named in underworld investigations (23 December 2003)
The Sydney Morning Herald: Williams 'feared' blame over Radev death (July 2007)
ABC News: Unsolved underworld killings, Victorian coroner closes probe into Melbourne gangland deaths (8 December 2016)
VICE: Australia's Most Notorious Hit Men (15 June 2018)
The Crime Chronicles: Nik Radev, Wannabe gangster (3 February 2019)

content.p: Nikolai Radev arrived in Australia as a refugee and spent most of the next two decades as a professional intimidator. Melbourne's police and underworld knew him as "Bulgarian Nick" or "The Russian". On the afternoon of Tuesday 15 April 2003 he was shot repeatedly in his black Mercedes in Queen Street, Coburg, in the northern suburbs of Melbourne. It happened just after 4.30 pm, according to The Age, and two associates who had driven to the street with him fled as the shots were fired.

His killing became one of the unsolved cases of Melbourne's gangland war. Police said within months that he had been lured to the street. Years later, they said they knew who pulled the trigger, but that the man had died before he could be charged. In December 2016 a coroner closed a summary inquest into the death without any charges being laid.

The Age reported in December 2003 that Radev was a young Bulgarian wrestler who reached Australia in 1980 with no assets and was granted refugee status. Australian authorities did not know his record from his early years in Bulgaria. The year after he arrived he married Sylvia, then training as a hairdresser. For a while he helped in her parents' Doveton fish-and-chip shop before setting up a pizza shop in Dandenong. The Crime Chronicles blog, which is not a news outlet, says he worked honestly for about two years.

The Age said that about a year into this he concluded that crime paid better, and that from 1983 until his death he neither worked nor paid tax, yet lived like a rich man. Soon after arriving he contacted members of Melbourne's Russian organised crime groups. His former wife told the paper he "wanted to be like Al Pacino in Scarface", that he told her he had married her only to obtain Australian citizenship, and that he "ended up just wasting his life".

His record, as The Age set it out, ran from drug trafficking in 1985 to a five-year sentence in 1987 for his part in a plan to blow up a convenience store. His Melbourne record also took in assaults, blackmail, death threats, extortion, weapons offences, armed robbery and drug cases. By the late 1990s he was trafficking heroin in St Kilda, and he was jailed again in 1999. The paper wrote that after time in Bulgarian prisons, Melbourne's jails were like weekend retreats to him.

Police told The Age that he had been the enforcer for the head of the Melbourne Russian mafia and a major drug trafficker, that he robbed drug dealers at gunpoint, and that he had access to a machine-gun. Some of the barristers who represented him said his refusal to pay his legal bills was another of his crimes. He had been a suspect in the killing of another underworld figure, Victor Peirce, and a close friend of the heroin dealer Peter Allen. The paper said he had also been briefly considered a suspect by the taskforce that investigated the murders of the police officers Gary Silk and Rodney Miller. In 1998 he and an associate, Housan "Sam" Zayat, had been charged over an invasion of a home where a 71-year-old man was beaten and his young granddaughter, aged five, was tied to a bed and threatened with a gun.
The Age also reported, citing police reports, that he had abducted and tortured the GST fraud suspect Sedat Ceylan while demanding $100,000. Ceylan fled to Turkey with his money.

From 2000, associates said, Radev "went up in the world". He rented a house in Brighton and paid the $530 rent in cash. He flew overseas five times in four years, always in business class. He lavished gifts on his de facto wife and child, yet did not live with them. A few weeks before his death he bought the black Mercedes for about $100,000. When he was killed he wore a $20,000 watch and a Versace outfit, shoes included.

The Crime Chronicles blog says he rarely left the Brighton house unarmed, and that April 2003 was an exception. Another version of his character came from his solicitor, George Balot, who said after the shooting that his client "was an honourable man". A former lawyer told The Age that Radev had always been pleasant to deal with. The writer Mark Brandon Read, a former underworld figure, said Radev was known to have run up large debts and that his attitude to personal accounting had always been "cavalier".
When he died he was the subject of a major drug investigation, police sources told The Age, and he was due to face assault and firearms charges in August.

According to The Age's account in December 2003, Radev drove from his Brighton home to meet a group of men at the Brighton Baths Cafe. He and some of the men then travelled in at least three cars to Coburg. Detectives believed he had been persuaded to go on the promise of a lucrative drug deal, and that the operation had been carefully planned.

Two men who had driven with him to Queen Street were interviewed by police. They said they heard the shots but did not see the shooting. The homicide squad's Detective Senior Sergeant Clive Rust appealed for witnesses. A witness at the scene had seen a small red sedan, possibly a Holden Vectra, near the corner of Queen and Reynard streets. The car left moments before the shooting. Police thought it was one of the vehicles that had come from Brighton, and that its two occupants left once they saw Radev had walked into the trap. The paper added that the father in a family amphetamine-making team was known to own a small red sedan, and that he and his son were under investigation over a series of unsolved gangland murders.

Police also said another man, implicated in at least four underworld shootings, had a meeting arranged with Radev that day. A later Age feature said the man known as "Benji", who had been implicated in several unsolved killings, met Radev on 15 April. The paper did not name him in that passage as the killer.

Radev was believed to have had more than $200,000 in cash hidden at his Brighton house. Police were told that his business associates took the money soon after the murder, claiming it was their share of the profits.

Radev was not the only person in his circle to die that year. Mark Mallia, 30, a standover man closely connected to him, was found as a charred body in West Sunshine on 18 August 2003. Another associate, Housan "Sam" Zayat, 32, was shot dead on 9 September in Tarneit, in Melbourne's west, a week before his committal hearing on drug charges was due to start.

In December 2003 detectives from the Purana taskforce named six men as "persons of interest" in their investigations. A detective told the Melbourne Magistrates Court that two of the six, Damien Cossu and Alfonso Traglia, were alleged to have been there when Radev was shot. Victoria's chief Crown prosecutor, Bill Morgan-Payler, QC, alleged Cossu was a close associate of both Radev and Mallia and that they were all involved in joint criminal enterprises. Nobody was charged with Radev's killing. By 2007 Cossu, then 31, was one of four men facing a committal hearing for Mallia's murder. His outcome is not given in the reports used here.

The Mallia case also produced a second theory of why Radev died. At that 2007 hearing the court heard statements from a witness identified only as Witness A, who said Carl Williams feared being blamed for Radev's death. According to Witness A, Mallia told Williams at a meeting at Crown Casino that he had heard rumours that Williams and Williams's close associate Andrew Veniamin were behind it. Williams denied it, the witness said, and Veniamin, who was present, threatened to kill Mallia and his family if he tried to take revenge. Witness A said Williams later arranged a $50,000 hit on Mallia. Williams, who had already pleaded guilty to murdering Mallia and two other underworld figures, received three life terms with a minimum of 35 years. The Sydney Morning Herald's report gives the date of Radev's death as August 2003. The Age and other outlets place it on 15 April, and the SMH date appears to be an error.
content.h2: Competing suspects and the screen version
content.p: VICE reported in 2018 that, according to police intelligence, Veniamin killed Benvenuto, Dino Dibra and then Radev, followed by Paul Kallipolitis, before what a long-time friend, Faruk Orman, described as his "crazy time". Veniamin was described there as a hitman who worked for Williams. The Age, writing in 2003, did not name any killer, and the 2016 ABC coverage said police had not revealed the identity of the man they believed responsible. VICE reported that Mick Gatto, a figure in the rival Carlton crew, was acquitted on grounds of self-defence after Veniamin was shot in a restaurant. VICE did not say that Veniamin's death was linked to Radev's killing.

The television series Underbelly, based on the book Leadbelly by the Age journalists John Silvester and Andrew Rule, dramatised Radev's death, with Williams ordering a hit by Veniamin and another man. A fan blog that catalogued the show's departures from the facts wrote that the series showed Radev killed late at night by two men, while in reality he was ambushed on a residential street in Coburg in the late afternoon. The blog said he was accompanied by two bodyguards. The Age's 2003 report spoke only of two associates.

The case returned to the public in December 2016, when a coronial inquiry into three unsolved gangland killings, those of Radev, Frank Benvenuto and Mario Condello, ended with no charges. The coroner held a summary, or short, inquest. ABC News reported that the information it released was all that police could reveal without risking future prosecutions.

On Radev, ABC reported that police believed they knew who killed him but that their suspect died in 2004, so no conviction was possible. Radev, whom the broadcaster described as 44, had supplied chemicals for an amphetamine production syndicate that included high-profile gangland criminals. An unidentified protected police witness told detectives that they drove the gunman to and from the shooting. Another protected witness, who was part of the drug syndicate, was also there. The shooter is believed to have used two handguns and kept firing after Radev fell.

Police said rising tension within the syndicate led several of its members to decide he should die. Detectives said that in the months before, Radev had told associates he needed to meet the amphetamine manufacturer because he was worried about the quality of the product. He was lured to Coburg on the pretext of such a meeting. Police did not name the gunman.

Within days of the shooting, The Age noted that there had been 13 underworld-related murders in Melbourne in the past five years, and all remained unsolved. He compared Radev with Freddie Harrison, a gangster shot dead on a Melbourne wharf in 1958 with about 30 men in the area, each of whom was to say he saw nothing. Police told the paper that witnesses refused to cooperate and that killers planned their crimes to leave few clues. A former homicide squad head, Carl Mengler, said such murders were hard but not impossible to solve, given time and resources.

The Crime Chronicles blog, which says it was written by a Queen Street resident, comments that Radev died alone and unpopular, with no crowd at his funeral. It called him "a pawn in a chess game he had no business being part of". The Age said his funeral would be held at the Macedonian Bulgarian Eastern Orthodox Church in Northcote. In 2016 the coroner closed the inquest without naming the gunman.
